    Field Theory

    Introduction

    Field theory is the theory of fields.

    The field theory involved in this article primarily focuses on field extensions. A field is an algebraic structure closed under addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division. In competitive programming, we often need to take modulo of a prime number 𝑝p, which is equivalent to performing operations in the finite field 𝐅𝑝Fp. Similar to the case of the real field 𝐑R, some problems become easier to solve in larger fields (namely the complex field 𝐂C). A common example is using Fast Fourier Transform to accelerate the multiplication of polynomials with real coefficients. Similar operations can be performed on finite fields. Since most readers are relatively unfamiliar with extensions of finite fields, understanding the general theory of field extensions is beneficial. At the end of this article, some algorithmic applications requiring field extensions are given, and briefly discusses extensions of integer rings that may be needed in some applications.

    Closely related to field theory is Galois theory. It connects field extensions with their automorphism groups, allowing one to understand the properties of field extensions through group theory tools. Although this theory is often the core of related algebra courses, it is far from the content of competitive programming, so this article does not provide excessive introduction. Interested readers should consult specialized textbooks.

    Notation

    When there is no ambiguity, this article may omit the multiplication symbol for rings and fields, and will write the ring (𝑅, +, ⋅)(R,+,⋅) as the ring 𝑅R, and the field (𝐹, +, ⋅)(F,+,⋅) as the field 𝐹F. The additive identity of a ring or field is called the zero element, and the multiplicative identity is called the unity element. Moreover, 𝑝p in this article is always a prime, and 𝑞q is always a prime power, which can be written as 𝑝𝑛pn, where 𝑛n is a positive integer.

    Field Extensions

    Similar to the cases of groups and rings, we can establish the concepts of subfields and field homomorphisms.

    Subfield

    For a field 𝐹F, if its subring 𝐸E is also a field, then 𝐸E is called a subfield of 𝐹F.

    Here, regardless of how rings and subrings handle the unity element, the subfield 𝐸E must contain the unity element of 𝐹F1.

    Field Homomorphism

    A ring homomorphism 𝜑 :𝐹 →𝐸φ:F→E from a field 𝐹F to a field 𝐸E is also called a field homomorphism from 𝐹F to 𝐸E.

    Field Homomorphisms and Unity Elements

    If, unlike the definition in this article, ring homomorphisms require the unity element to map to the unity element, then field homomorphisms naturally require the unity element to map to the unity element. Otherwise, the unity element may also map to the zero element.

    Since fields only have trivial ideals, a field homomorphism either maps the entire field to the zero element or must be an embedding. This shows that the discussion of field homomorphisms can be transformed into the discussion of subfields.

    In the case of fields, the smaller field is often more familiar, so we usually examine larger fields with respect to subfields. This leads to the concept of field extensions.

    Field Extension

    For fields 𝐹F and 𝐸E, if 𝐹F is a subfield of 𝐸E, then 𝐸E is called an extension of 𝐹F, also called an extension field, denoted 𝐸/𝐹E/F.

    Notation for Field Extensions

    Although the notation is the same, the concept of field extensions has no relation to quotient rings and should not be confused.

    Examples

    The complex field 𝐂C is an extension of the real field 𝐑R, and 𝐑R is an extension of the rational field 𝐐Q.

    Degree of Field Extensions

    For a field extension 𝐸/𝐹E/F, 𝐸E is always a linear space over 𝐹F. The dimension of this linear space is the degree of the field extension.

    Degree of Field Extension

    The degree of a field extension 𝐸/𝐹E/F is the dimension of 𝐸E considered as a linear space over 𝐹F, namely dim𝐹⁡(𝐸)dimF⁡(E), denoted [𝐸 :𝐹][E:F]. If the degree is finite, the extension is called a finite extension; otherwise, it is called an infinite extension.

    Examples

    The degree of the extension 𝐂/𝐑C/R is [𝐂 :𝐑] =2[C:R]=2, so it is a finite extension. 𝐑/𝐐R/Q is an infinite extension.

    The degree of field extensions satisfies the multiplication formula.

    Theorem

    Let 𝐹 ⊆𝐾 ⊆𝐸F⊆K⊆E all be fields, then the degrees satisfy [𝐸 :𝐹] =[𝐸 :𝐾][𝐾 :𝐹][E:F]=[E:K][K:F].

    Proof

    For infinite degree, this is obvious; otherwise, if {𝛼𝑖}{αi} is a basis of 𝐸E as a linear space over 𝐾K, and {𝛽𝑗}{βj} is a basis of 𝐾K as a linear space over 𝐹F, then one can verify that {𝛼𝑖𝛽𝑗}{αiβj} is a basis of 𝐸E as a linear space over 𝐹F.

    The discussion in this article primarily focuses on finite field extensions.

    Characteristic of a Field

    A natural starting point for studying field extensions is the smallest subfield containing the unity element of 𝐹F, which is also called the prime subfield of 𝐹F.

    The structure of the prime subfield is uniquely determined by the properties of the unity element of the field. The characteristic of a field summarizes such properties.

    Characteristic of a Field

    The characteristic of a field 𝐹F is the smallest positive integer 𝑛n such that 𝑛 ⋅1 =0n⋅1=0; if such 𝑛n does not exist, the characteristic of 𝐹F is 00. Here, 𝑛 ⋅1n⋅1 means the sum of 𝑛n unity elements 11. If the characteristic of 𝐹F is not 00, then 𝐹F is said to have finite characteristic.

    The characteristic of a field can be understood through ring homomorphisms. The integer ring 𝐙Z is the closed structure obtained starting from 00 and 11 by repeatedly applying addition, subtraction, and multiplication. It can be considered as a kind of "prototype", and all rings containing the unity element should "inherit" some structure of the integer ring2. Therefore, for a field 𝐹F, we can consider the ring homomorphism 𝜑 :𝐙 →𝐹φ:Z→F with 𝜑(1) =1φ(1)=1. Such a ring homomorphism is uniquely determined, mapping 𝑛 ∈𝐍+n∈N+ to 𝑛 ⋅1n⋅1, the sum of 𝑛n unity elements 11. The image 𝜑(𝐙)φ(Z) embedded in 𝐹F necessarily contains the unity, is commutative, and has no zero divisors, so it is an integral domain. Hence, the kernel ker⁡𝜑ker⁡φ must be a prime ideal. The prime ideals of 𝐙Z can only be of the form (𝑛)(n), where 𝑛 =0n=0 or 𝑛n is a prime. The 𝑛n obtained is the characteristic of the field.

    The characteristic determines the structure of the prime subfield:

    1. When the characteristic is 00, 𝜑φ is injective, and 𝐙Z is embedded in 𝐹F. The field of rational numbers 𝐐Q as the smallest field containing 𝐙Z can also be embedded in 𝐹F, and it is the prime subfield of 𝐹F;
    2. When the characteristic is a prime 𝑝p, the image 𝐙/𝑝𝐙Z/pZ is embedded in 𝐹F. At this point, 𝐙/𝑝𝐙Z/pZ is already a field, denoted 𝐅𝑝Fp, and it is the prime subfield of 𝐹F.

    These discussions actually prove the following conclusion:

    Theorem

    The characteristic of a field 𝐹F can only be 00 or a prime 𝑝p. The prime subfield of a field with characteristic 00 is 𝐐Q, and the prime subfield of a field with characteristic 𝑝p is 𝐅𝑝Fp.

    The 𝐐Q and 𝐅𝑝Fp in the theorem are also called prime fields, that is, fields whose only subfield is themselves. Finite fields necessarily have finite characteristic, because fields with characteristic 00 contain at least the subfield 𝐐Q.

    Fields with finite characteristic and those with characteristic zero often have different properties. For example, fields with finite characteristic have the following properties:

    Theorem

    Let the characteristic of 𝐹F be 𝑝p, then:

    1. In the additive group of 𝐹F, all non-zero elements have order 𝑝p, that is, 𝑝𝑥 =0px=0 for all 𝑥 ∈𝐹x∈F;
    2. The "freshman's dream": for all 𝑥,𝑦 ∈𝐹x,y∈F, (𝑥 +𝑦)𝑝 =𝑥𝑝 +𝑦𝑝(x+y)p=xp+yp. Furthermore, the map 𝑥 ↦𝑥𝑝x↦xp is an injective endomorphism of 𝐹F, called the Frobenius endomorphism.
    Proof

    For the first property, note that 𝑝𝑥 =(𝑝1)𝑥 =0𝑥 =0px=(p1)x=0x=0. For the second property, note that in the binomial expansion of (𝑥 +𝑦)𝑝(x+y)p, all other coefficients besides 𝑥𝑝xp and 𝑦𝑝yp are multiples of 𝑝p, so by the first property, (𝑥 +𝑦)𝑝 =𝑥𝑝 +𝑦𝑝(x+y)p=xp+yp. To verify that 𝑥 ↦𝑥𝑝x↦xp is an endomorphism, we only need to verify (𝑥𝑦)𝑝 =𝑥𝑝𝑦𝑝(xy)p=xpyp, which holds because field multiplication is commutative. Finally, a ring homomorphism between fields mapping the unity element to the unity element must be injective.

    Of course, for finite fields, the Frobenius endomorphism is also surjective, and thus is a field automorphism.

    Simple Extensions

    Similar to extending the real field to the complex field, many extensions can be completed by adding additional elements to the field and specifying their algebraic properties. In general, to avoid complications from specifying algebraic properties, we can consider adding elements from 𝐸 ∖𝐹E∖F to 𝐹F in the extension 𝐸/𝐹E/F, where the rules for operations between these additional elements and elements of 𝐹F are already determined in the larger field 𝐸E.

    Extension Generated by a Subset

    Let 𝐸/𝐹E/F be a field extension and 𝑆 ⊆𝐸S⊆E. The extension generated by 𝑆S over 𝐹F is the smallest subfield of 𝐸E containing both 𝐹F and 𝑆S, denoted 𝐹(𝑆)F(S).

    The simplest case is when the set 𝑆S has few elements.

    Finitely Generated Extension

    Let 𝐸/𝐹E/F be a field extension. If there exists a finite set 𝑆 ={𝛼1,⋯,𝛼𝑛} ⊆𝐸S={α1,⋯,αn}⊆E such that 𝐸 =𝐹(𝑆)E=F(S), then 𝐸E is called a finitely generated extension of 𝐹F, also denoted 𝐹(𝛼1,⋯,𝛼𝑛)F(α1,⋯,αn).

    Simple Extension

    Let 𝐸/𝐹E/F be a field extension. If there exists 𝛼 ∈𝐸α∈E such that 𝐸 =𝐹(𝛼)E=F(α), then 𝐸E is called a simple extension of 𝐹F. The element 𝛼α is called a primitive element of this simple extension.

    Examples

    These examples are all obtained by adding elements of 𝐂C to 𝐐Q:

    1. For a square-free integer 𝐷 ≠0,1D≠0,1, the quadratic field 𝐐(√𝐷)Q(D) is obtained by adding √𝐷 ∈𝐂 ∖𝐐D∈C∖Q to 𝐐Q. It is a simple extension with degree 22, because {1,√𝐷}{1,D} forms a basis.
    2. The field 𝐐(√2,√3)Q(2,3) is obtained by adding √22 and √33 to 𝐐Q. Of course, 𝐐(√2,√3) =𝐐(√2)(√3) =𝐐(√3)(√2)Q(2,3)=Q(2)(3)=Q(3)(2), meaning the final extension is independent of the order and method of adding elements. This is also a simple extension because 𝐐(√2,√3) =𝐐(√2 +√3)Q(2,3)=Q(2+3). Its degree is 44, because {1,√2,√3,√6}{1,2,3,6} forms a basis.
    3. The field 𝐐(𝜋)Q(π) is also a simple extension, where 𝜋π is the circumference ratio. It is an infinite extension because 𝐐[𝜋] ⊆𝐐(𝜋)Q[π]⊆Q(π) already has a basis {1,𝜋,𝜋2,⋯}{1,π,π2,⋯}.
    4. The field 𝐐(𝜋,e)Q(π,e) is a finitely generated extension but not a simple extension. Here, 𝜋π is the circumference ratio, and ee is the base of the natural logarithm.

    These examples show that the properties of simple extensions can vary greatly. This depends on the nature of the added elements.

    Algebraic Extensions

    To analyze all possible cases of adding elements to a field, we can, following the earlier discussion on the characteristic of a field, consider ring homomorphisms from the polynomial ring 𝐹[𝑥]F[x] to the extension 𝐸/𝐹E/F. Here, 𝐹[𝑥]F[x] serves the same role as the integer ring 𝐙Z discussed earlier: it is the "prototype" of the structure formed by adding an indeterminate 𝑥x to the field 𝐹F and closing under addition, subtraction, and multiplication3.

    Let 𝜑 :𝐹[𝑥] →𝐸φ:F[x]→E be a ring homomorphism such that 𝜑φ restricted to 𝐹F is the identity map, and 𝜑(𝑥) =𝛼φ(x)=α, that is, mapping the indeterminate to some element 𝛼α in the extension 𝐸E. At this time, since the image 𝜑(𝐹[𝑥]) =𝐹[𝛼]φ(F[x])=F[α] is necessarily an integral domain, the kernel ker⁡𝜑ker⁡φ must be a prime ideal of the polynomial ring 𝐹[𝑥]F[x]. The polynomial ring over a field is a principal ideal domain, so it must have the form (𝑓(𝑥))(f(x)), where 𝑓(𝑥) =0f(x)=0 or 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) is an irreducible element of 𝐹[𝑥]F[x]. The discussion is as follows:

    1. When ker⁡𝜑 ={0}ker⁡φ={0}, the polynomial ring 𝐹[𝑥]F[x] is embedded into 𝐸E, and its image 𝐹[𝛼]F[α] is an integral domain. Therefore, the smallest field in 𝐸E containing both 𝐹F and 𝛼α is the fraction field of 𝐹[𝛼]F[α], namely 𝐹(𝛼)F(α). This notation can be interpreted either as substituting 𝛼α for the indeterminate in the rational function field 𝐹(𝑥)F(x), or as the simple extension of 𝐹F generated by 𝛼α; these two interpretations yield the same result in this context;

    2. When ker⁡𝜑 =(𝑓(𝑥))ker⁡φ=(f(x)) and 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) is irreducible, then 𝜑(𝑓(𝑥)) =𝑓(𝛼) =0φ(f(x))=f(α)=0, that is, 𝛼 ∈𝐸α∈E is a root of the polynomial 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) over 𝐹F. Since 𝐹F is a field, let 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) be a monic polynomial. At this time, the image of 𝜑φ is the field 𝐹(𝛼)F(α), so we have

      𝐹[𝑥]/(𝑓(𝑥))≅𝐹(𝛼).F[x]/(f(x))≅F(α).

      This can be divided into two cases:

      1. If 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) is a linear polynomial, that is, 𝑓(𝑥) =𝑥 −𝛼f(x)=x−α, then 𝛼 ∈𝐹α∈F, so the extension 𝐹(𝛼) =𝐹F(α)=F is trivial;
      2. In other cases, 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) is an irreducible polynomial of degree greater than one, and 𝛼 ∈𝐸 ∖𝐹α∈E∖F. At this time, 𝐹[𝛼]F[α] already contains 𝐹F and 𝛼α, so it is 𝐹(𝛼)F(α), the extension of 𝐹F generated by 𝛼α, and 𝐹(𝛼) ⊃𝐹F(α)⊃F is nontrivial.

    This discussion leads to the following definitions:

    Algebraic and Transcendental Elements

    For an extension 𝐸/𝐹E/F, if an element 𝛼 ∈𝐸α∈E is a root of some non-zero polynomial 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) over 𝐹F, then 𝛼α is called an algebraic element over 𝐹F; otherwise, 𝛼α is called a transcendental element over 𝐹F.

    Minimal Polynomial

    For an algebraic element 𝛼α over a field 𝐹F, the monic polynomial 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) of smallest degree having 𝛼α as a root is called its minimal polynomial.

    The minimal polynomial here is exactly the irreducible polynomial 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) from the earlier analysis. Of course, it can also be directly proven that minimal polynomials are all irreducible. The minimality of 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) means that any polynomial over 𝐹F having 𝛼α as a root must contain 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) as a factor.

    Examples
    1. √22 is algebraic over 𝐐Q, with minimal polynomial 𝑥2 −2x2−2.
    2. √22 is algebraic over 𝐑R, with minimal polynomial 𝑥 −√2x−2.
    3. 𝜋π is transcendental over 𝐐Q.
    4. In general, algebraic elements over 𝐐Q are called algebraic numbers, while transcendental elements are called transcendental numbers. Particularly, if the minimal polynomial of an algebraic number is a monic polynomial, it is called an algebraic integer. All algebraic integers in an algebraic extension form a ring. For example, the algebraic integers in the quadratic field 𝐐(√𝐷)Q(D) form the quadratic integer ring 𝐙[𝜔]Z[ω]. See Quadratic Integer Rings for the meaning of this notation.
    Algebraic and Transcendental Extensions

    For an extension 𝐸/𝐹E/F, if all elements of 𝐸E are algebraic over 𝐹F, then 𝐸E is called an algebraic extension of 𝐹F; otherwise, 𝐸E is called a transcendental extension of 𝐹F.

    The results of simple extensions can be divided into two categories based on the nature of the added element. When the added element is transcendental, the simple extension is always isomorphic to the rational function field. At this time, there is no possibility for further simplification. However, when the added element is algebraic, the simple extension is actually 𝐹[𝛼]F[α], that is, the result of directly replacing the indeterminate 𝑥x in the polynomial ring 𝐹[𝑥]F[x] with 𝛼α. From an elementary perspective, compared to transcendental elements, elements in the extension field in the case of algebraic simple extensions can have no denominators; this means that the process similar to "rationalizing denominators" in elementary arithmetic is always feasible in algebraic simple extensions. Since the extension fields involved in competitive programming are primarily simple algebraic extensions, the next section will discuss their computation in more detail.

    The importance of simple algebraic extensions is also reflected in the following theorem:

    Theorem

    A field extension is finite if and only if it is a finitely generated algebraic extension.

    Proof

    Let 𝐹F be a field, and 𝐸 =𝐹(𝛼1,⋯,𝛼𝑛)E=F(α1,⋯,αn) be a finitely generated algebraic extension over 𝐹F, where each 𝛼𝑖αi is algebraic over 𝐹F. Let 𝐸𝑖 =𝐹(𝛼1,⋯,𝛼𝑖)Ei=F(α1,⋯,αi), then 𝐸0 =𝐹E0=F and 𝐸𝑛 =𝐸En=E. Note that 𝛼𝑖αi must be algebraic over 𝐸𝑖−1Ei−1, because the minimal polynomial of 𝛼𝑖αi over 𝐹F is also a polynomial over 𝐸𝑖−1Ei−1; moreover, the degree of the minimal polynomial of 𝛼𝑖αi over 𝐸𝑖−1Ei−1 cannot exceed that over 𝐹F. Therefore, [𝐸𝑖 :𝐸𝑖−1][Ei:Ei−1] is necessarily finite, and by the multiplication formula for degrees of field extensions, [𝐸 :𝐹] =∏𝑛𝑖=1[𝐸𝑖 :𝐸𝑖−1][E:F]=∏i=1n[Ei:Ei−1] is also finite. Conversely, starting from 𝐸0 =𝐹E0=F, for each constructed 𝐸𝑖Ei, we can choose an element 𝛼𝑖+1 ∈𝐸 ∖𝐸𝑖αi+1∈E∖Ei to add to 𝐸𝑖Ei, obtaining 𝐸𝑖+1 =𝐸𝑖(𝛼𝑖+1)Ei+1=Ei(αi+1), until 𝐸𝑛 =𝐸En=E. Since the degree of the extension keeps decreasing, this process must terminate in a finite number of steps. Therefore, finite extensions are necessarily finitely generated algebraic extensions.

    This means that to understand the properties of finite extensions, one only needs to understand simple algebraic extensions. Since finite extensions can always be obtained through finitely many simple algebraic extensions.

    Structure and Computation of Simple Algebraic Extensions

    In this section, let 𝐹F be a number field, 𝐸E its extension field, and 𝛼 ∈𝐸 ∖𝐹α∈E∖F be algebraic over 𝐹F. Let the minimal polynomial of 𝛼α be 𝑓(𝑥)f(x), and let 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) be an 𝑛n-degree monic polynomial, that is,

    𝑓(𝑥)=𝑥𝑛+𝑎𝑛−1𝑥𝑛−1+⋯+𝑎1𝑥+𝑎0,f(x)=xn+an−1xn−1+⋯+a1x+a0,

    where 𝑎0,𝑎1,⋯,𝑎𝑛−1 ∈𝐹a0,a1,⋯,an−1∈F and 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) is irreducible over 𝐹F.

    The isomorphism 𝐹(𝛼) ≅𝐹[𝑥]/(𝑓(𝑥))F(α)≅F[x]/(f(x)) indicates that the operations in the extension field 𝐹(𝛼)F(α) are just computations of polynomials modulo 𝑓(𝑥)f(x). According to polynomial division with remainder, we only need to consider all congruence classes of polynomials with degree less than 𝑛 =deg⁡𝑓(𝑥)n=deg⁡f(x). For these polynomials, a natural basis is {1,𝛼,⋯,𝛼𝑛−1}{1,α,⋯,αn−1}. Therefore, we have the following theorem:

In the extension field, the addition of elements 𝜆(𝛼)λ(α) and 𝜇(𝛼)μ(α) is just polynomial addition, that is, adding coefficients at corresponding positions; the multiplication of 𝜆(𝛼)λ(α) and 𝜇(𝛼)μ(α) can be written as 𝜌(𝛼)ρ(α), where 𝜌(𝑥)ρ(x) is the remainder of 𝜆(𝑥)𝜇(𝑥)λ(x)μ(x) divided by 𝑓(𝑥)f(x).

    Of course, as a field, we can also compute division in 𝐹(𝛼)F(α). According to the multiplication process described in the theorem, this is equivalent to solving a linear congruence equation over polynomial rings. Analogous to the integer case, to compute the quotient 𝜆(𝛼)/𝜇(𝛼)λ(α)/μ(α), we can first determine the multiplicative inverse of 𝜇(𝛼)μ(α), then multiply by 𝜆(𝛼)λ(α). To compute the multiplicative inverse of 𝜇(𝛼)μ(α), we just need to solve the congruence equation 𝜇(𝑥)𝜉(𝑥) ≡1(mod𝑓(𝑥))μ(x)ξ(x)≡1(modf(x)). This can be achieved through the extended Euclidean algorithm.

The polynomial 𝑥3 −2𝑥 −2 =0x3−2x−2=0 has one real root and a pair of conjugate complex roots in the complex field 𝐂C. The extension fields obtained by adding any of them to the rational field 𝐐Q are all isomorphic. That is, these three distinct roots are not different from an algebraic perspective.

    In general, for an irreducible polynomial 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) over a field 𝐹F, in the extension field there are different roots 𝛼 ≠𝛽α≠β. The usual notion of conjugates over the complex field is a special case of this concept for the field extension 𝐂/𝐑C/R.

    Consider the extension field 𝐅2(𝛼)F2(α), where 𝛼α is a root of the equation 𝑥2 +𝑥 +1 =0x2+x+1=0. In general, for 𝑎 +𝑏𝛼a+bα and 𝑐 +𝑑𝛼c+dα, the arithmetic rules are

    (𝑎+𝑏𝛼)+(𝑐+𝑑𝛼)=(𝑎+𝑐)+(𝑏+𝑑)𝛼,(𝑎+𝑏𝛼)(𝑐+𝑑𝛼)=𝑎𝑐+(𝑎𝑑+𝑏𝑐)𝛼+𝑏𝑑𝛼2=(𝑎𝑐+𝑏𝑑)+(𝑎𝑑+𝑏𝑐+𝑏𝑑)𝛼.(a+bα)+(c+dα)=(a+c)+(b+d)α,(a+bα)(c+dα)=ac+(ad+bc)α+bdα2=(ac+bd)+(ad+bc+bd)α.

    This provides arithmetic rules similar to those over the complex field. Most readers should be unfamiliar with such roots 𝛼α, but this does not prevent performing operations on elements in such a field. In fact, [𝐅2(𝛼) :𝐅2] =2[F2(α):F2]=2, so as a linear space, |𝐅2(𝛼)| =4|F2(α)|=4, that is, the finite field of size 44 is obtained. Later, we will see that all finite fields are constructed in this way.

    For small-scale computations, operations modulo the monic polynomial 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) can often be performed by substituting

    𝑥𝑛=−𝑎𝑛−1𝑥𝑛−1−⋯−𝑎1𝑥−𝑎0xn=−an−1xn−1−⋯−a1x−a0

    to reduce the degree of the target polynomial. Moreover, for low-degree extensions, the arithmetic rules for coefficients can often be computed directly, using an implementation similar to complex number classes without computing modulo each time.

    As an example of simple algebraic extensions, refer to the reference implementation below.

    The algorithms described here can only handle extensions of low degree in practice, which is sufficient for most applications in competitive programming. For cases where the degree becomes a bottleneck, appropriate polynomial techniques (Fast Fourier Transform, Number-Theoretic Transform, Polynomial Fast Remainder, Polynomial Euclidean Algorithm etc.) should be used to accelerate computations.

    Splitting Fields

    The structure of simple algebraic extensions has been discussed in detail above. However, such extensions are often insufficient:

    Examples

    Consider the extension 𝐐(3√2)/𝐐Q(23)/Q. The algebraic element 3√223 has minimal polynomial 𝑥3 −2x3−2 over 𝐐Q. In the complex field 𝐂C, the polynomial 𝑥3 −2x3−2 has three roots: 3√2,3√2𝜔,3√2𝜔223,23ω,23ω2, where 𝜔 =e2𝜋i/3ω=e2πi/3 is a primitive third root of unity. Although 𝐐(3√2) ≅𝐐(3√2𝜔) ≅𝐐(3√2𝜔2)Q(23)≅Q(23ω)≅Q(23ω2), 𝐐(3√2)Q(23) does not contain the other two roots, making operations like 3√2 +3√2𝜔23+23ω impossible. To completely examine these three roots, further extension of 𝐐(3√2)Q(23) is needed, extending to 𝐐(3√2,3√2𝜔,3√2𝜔2)Q(23,23ω,23ω2).

    As shown earlier, to make such an extension, we can perform simple extensions on elements one by one. It should be noted that the minimal polynomial of 3√2𝜔23ω over 𝐐Q and over 𝐐(3√2)Q(23) is not the same: the former is 𝑥3 −2 ∈𝐐[𝑥]x3−2∈Q[x], while the latter is 𝑥2 +3√2𝑥 +3√4 ∈𝐐(3√2)[𝑥]x2+23x+43∈Q(23)[x], because

    𝑥3−2=(𝑥−3√2)(𝑥2+3√2𝑥+3√4).x3−2=(x−23)(x2+23x+43).

    The original minimal polynomial factorizes into linear factors after the field extension, so the degree of the minimal polynomial of the remaining roots is lower than that over the original field. The process of continuously extending the field is the process of continuously "splitting" polynomials. Therefore, when performing each simple extension, the minimal polynomial needs to be redetermined.

    Adding all roots of a polynomial to the field gives the splitting field of the polynomial.

    Split

    Let 𝐹F be a field. If a polynomial 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) in 𝐹[𝑥]F[x] can be factored into a product of linear factors, then 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) is said to split in 𝐹F.

    Splitting Field

    For a polynomial 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) over a field 𝐹F, if an extension 𝐸/𝐹E/F satisfies that 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) splits in 𝐸E but not in any proper subfield of 𝐸E, then 𝐸E is called the splitting field of 𝑓(𝑥)f(x).

    It can be proven that, like simple extensions, the splitting field of a given polynomial is uniquely determined up to isomorphism, independent of the specific construction method. Splitting fields are always finite extensions.

    Normal Extension

    For an algebraic extension 𝐸/𝐹E/F, if for all 𝛼 ∈𝐸α∈E, the minimal polynomial of 𝛼α splits in 𝐸E, then 𝐸E is called a normal extension of 𝐹F.

    Normal extensions play a fundamental role in Galois theory.

    Algebraically Closed Fields

    Most extension concepts discussed earlier should, in principle, be carried out inside a field larger than the extension. Although for simple extensions, extensions can be constructed without relying on larger fields through polynomial rings, there is no such method for general cases. For the rational field 𝐐Q and real field 𝐑R, we can always assume that algebraic extensions are contained within the complex field 𝐂C. For finite fields, there is no similar known field. In fact, for all fields, there exists an algebraic closure, so that all algebraic extensions over a field can be assumed to be within the algebraic closure. This completely resolves the issue.

    Algebraic Closure

    For a field 𝐹F, if ――𝐹F― is an algebraic extension of 𝐹F and all 𝑓(𝑥) ∈𝐹[𝑥]f(x)∈F[x] split in ――𝐹F―, then ――𝐹F― is called the algebraic closure of 𝐹F.

    The algebraic closure is a normal extension over the field. Its construction method is basically to add all possible polynomial roots to the field. And like splitting fields, the algebraic closure of a field is also unique up to isomorphism.

    Theorem

    Any field 𝐹F has an algebraic closure.

    Proof

    The difficulty of the proof comes from set theory. Here we cite a proof by Artin.

    The first part of the proof starts from 𝐹F, constructing an extension 𝐾1/𝐹K1/F such that all polynomials over 𝐹F have at least one root in 𝐾1K1. For a field 𝐹F, consider the multivariate polynomial ring10 𝑅 =𝐹[⋯,𝑥𝑓,⋯]R=F[⋯,xf,⋯], where the indeterminates 𝑥𝑓xf are indexed by all monic polynomials over 𝐹F. At this time, the ideal generated by all 𝑓(𝑥𝑓)f(xf) is denoted 𝐼I. First, 𝐼 ≠𝑅I≠R, so a maximal ideal 𝑀 ⊇𝐼M⊇I exists. Otherwise, if 1 ∈𝐼1∈I, there must exist finitely many monic polynomials 𝑓𝑖fi over 𝐹F and corresponding elements 𝑔𝑖gi in 𝑅R such that 𝑔1𝑓1(𝑥𝑓1) +⋯ +𝑔𝑘𝑓𝑘(𝑥𝑓𝑘) =1g1f1(xf1)+⋯+gkfk(xfk)=1 holds. Let 𝐹(𝛼1,⋯,𝛼𝑘)F(α1,⋯,αk) be the algebraic extension obtained by adding the roots 𝛼𝑖αi of 𝑓𝑖(𝑥)fi(x) to 𝐹F. Then, substituting 𝛼𝑖αi for 𝑥𝑓𝑖xfi in the above identity, and substituting 00 for all other indeterminates 𝑥𝑓xf appearing in 𝑔𝑖gi, we get the equation 0 =10=1 over 𝐹(𝛼1,⋯,𝛼𝑘)F(α1,⋯,αk), which is a contradiction. Therefore, 𝐼 ≠𝑅I≠R, and the construction of the maximal ideal 𝑀M is valid. At this time, the quotient ring 𝑅/𝑀R/M is a field, denoted 𝐾1K1, and any monic polynomial 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) over 𝐹F has a root ―――𝑥𝑓xf― in 𝐾1K1.

    The second part of the proof obtains an algebraic closure 𝐾K containing 𝐹F (definition below) through induction. Repeating the above construction, based on the field 𝐾𝑖Ki, we can construct 𝐾𝑖+1Ki+1 such that all polynomials of 𝐾𝑖Ki have at least one root in 𝐾𝑖+1Ki+1. Moreover, 𝐾𝑖Ki naturally embeds into 𝐾𝑖+1Ki+1, so we can define their union 𝐾 =⋃∞𝑖=1𝐾𝑖K=⋃i=1∞Ki. It is easy to verify that this is also a field, and all coefficients of any polynomial over 𝐾K are necessarily contained in some 𝐾𝑖Ki, so one of its roots necessarily appears in 𝐾𝑖+1 ⊆𝐾Ki+1⊆K. This shows that all polynomials over 𝐾K have at least one root in 𝐾K, so 𝐾K is an algebraically closed field.

    Finally, let ――𝐹F― be the set of all algebraic elements over 𝐹F in 𝐾K. It is obviously a field; because for any 𝛼,𝛽 ∈――𝐹α,β∈F―, we have 𝛼 ±𝛽,𝛼𝛽,𝛼/𝛽 ∈𝐹(𝛼,𝛽) ⊆――𝐹α±β,αβ,α/β∈F(α,β)⊆F―. It is also an algebraic extension of 𝐹F, because its elements are all algebraic over 𝐹F. For a polynomial 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) over 𝐹F, all its roots are algebraic over 𝐹F, so they are also in ――𝐹F―, and therefore can be factored into products of linear factors. This shows that ――𝐹F― is the algebraic closure of 𝐹F over 𝐹F.

    Examples
    1. The algebraic closure of the real field 𝐑R is the complex field 𝐂C.
    2. The algebraic closure of the rational field 𝐐Q is the set of all algebraic numbers (i.e., algebraic elements in the field extension 𝐂/𝐐C/Q), denoted ――𝐐Q―.

    All algebraic extensions of algebraic closures are trivial. Such fields are called algebraically closed fields.

    Algebraically Closed Field

    If every non-constant polynomial 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) over a field 𝐹F has at least one root 𝛼 ∈𝐹α∈F, then 𝐹F is called an algebraically closed field.

    In fact, it has the following equivalent definitions:

    Theorem

    For a field 𝐹F, the following properties are all equivalent:

    1. 𝐹F is algebraically closed;
    2. All polynomials 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) over 𝐹F split;
    3. The only irreducible polynomials over 𝐹F are linear polynomials;
    4. 𝐹F has no non-trivial algebraic extensions;
    5. 𝐹F has no non-trivial finite extensions;
    6. 𝐹F is the algebraic closure of some field.
    Proof

    The equivalence of the first five properties is obvious from the definitions. For the sixth, an algebraically closed field is obviously its own algebraic closure because it has no non-trivial algebraic extensions; conversely, to prove that the algebraic closure of 𝐹F is algebraically closed. Let ――𝐹F― be the algebraic closure of 𝐹F, and 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) a polynomial over ――𝐹F―. Let 𝛼α be a root of 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) in the splitting field of 𝑓(𝑥)f(x), and let the set of non-zero coefficients of 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) be 𝑆 ⊆――𝐹S⊆F―. Then, since 𝐹(𝑆)(𝛼) =𝐹(𝑆 ∪{𝛼})F(S)(α)=F(S∪{α}) is a finite extension, 𝛼α is also algebraic over 𝐹F, so according to the definition of algebraic closure, the minimal polynomial of 𝛼α over 𝐹F splits in ――𝐹F―, hence 𝛼 ∈――𝐹α∈F―. This shows that any polynomial over ――𝐹F― has at least one root.

    Finally, the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra 4 shows that 𝐂C is algebraically closed. Irreducible polynomials over 𝐑R are at most quadratic, or equivalently, the largest field obtainable through algebraic extensions is 𝐂C.

    Separable Extensions

    The concept of splitting fields guarantees that for any polynomial over any field, there is an extension field containing all its roots, and the splitting field precisely gives such the smallest extension field. The properties of polynomials are closely related to the properties of their splitting fields. However, if one hopes to study the properties of polynomials through their splitting fields, the first problem to face is that the splitting field of a polynomial is unrelated to the multiplicities of the polynomial's roots. Therefore, if possible, we should consider some kind of "simplest representation" of the polynomial. Inspired by this, we call polynomials that have no multiple roots in the algebraic closure of the field separable polynomials.

    Separable Polynomial

    For a polynomial 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) over a field 𝐹F, if 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) has no multiple roots in the algebraic closure ――𝐹F― of 𝐹F, that is, when it factors into a product of linear factors there are no repeated factors, then 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) is called separable.

    Since we always need to extend to the algebraic closure of 𝐹F to discuss separable polynomials, the determination of separable polynomials is actually independent of the choice of field 𝐹F. However, because the coefficients of polynomials are in 𝐹F, we should provide a method to determine whether a polynomial is separable over 𝐹F without explicitly constructing its extension field.

    Readers familiar with analysis know that multiple roots of polynomial functions can be determined through their derivatives: multiple roots of polynomial functions are also roots of their derivatives. Although polynomials and polynomial functions are not the same concept, the method for determining multiple roots of polynomial functions can be analogously applied to polynomials. The derivative of a polynomial can be defined formally as follows:

    Formal Derivative

    The (formal) derivative of a polynomial over 𝐹F

    𝑓(𝑥)=𝑎0+𝑎1𝑥+𝑎2𝑥2+⋯+𝑎𝑛−1𝑥𝑛−1+𝑎𝑛𝑥𝑛=𝑛∑𝑖=0𝑎𝑖𝑥𝑖f(x)=a0+a1x+a2x2+⋯+an−1xn−1+anxn=∑i=0naixi

    , denoted 𝐷𝑓(𝑥)Df(x), is defined as the polynomial

    𝐷𝑓(𝑥)=𝑎1+2𝑎2𝑥+⋯+(𝑛−1)𝑎𝑛−1𝑥𝑛−1+𝑛𝑎𝑛𝑥𝑛−1=𝑛∑𝑖=1𝑖𝑎𝑖𝑥𝑖−1.Df(x)=a1+2a2x+⋯+(n−1)an−1xn−1+nanxn−1=∑i=1niaixi−1.

    This definition applies to all polynomials over any field and does not depend on any topological structure. The derivative operator 𝐷D here just maps one polynomial to another. Moreover, by comparing coefficients, one can verify that the usual derivative rules, such as 𝐷(𝑓(𝑥)𝑔(𝑥)) =(𝐷𝑓(𝑥))𝑔(𝑥) +𝑓(𝑥)(𝐷𝑔(𝑥))D(f(x)g(x))=(Df(x))g(x)+f(x)(Dg(x)), still hold for formal derivatives.

    Furthermore, to check whether the polynomial 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) and its derivative 𝐷𝑓(𝑥)Df(x) have the same roots in the splitting field, we can not explicitly construct this splitting field, but determine it by their greatest common divisor; this is because polynomial roots always appear in its minimal polynomial, and repeated roots mean the corresponding minimal polynomial factors are also repeated. Therefore, we have the following criterion for multiple roots:

    Theorem

    For a polynomial 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) over a field 𝐹F, if 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) has a multiple root 𝛼α, then the derivative 𝐷𝑓(𝑥)Df(x) also has the same root 𝛼α. Furthermore, 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) is separable if and only if 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) and its derivative 𝐷𝑓(𝑥)Df(x) are coprime, that is, gcd(𝑓(𝑥),𝐷𝑓(𝑥)) =1gcd(f(x),Df(x))=1.

    Proof

    First, because Euclidean division still holds in extension fields, the results of the Euclidean algorithm are independent of the choice of extension field, so we only need to discuss their common factors in the splitting field. Thus, assuming 𝛼α is a root of 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) with multiplicity 𝑘 >1k>1, in the splitting field we have 𝑓(𝑥) =(𝑥 −𝛼)𝑘𝑔(𝑥)f(x)=(x−α)kg(x), so its derivative 𝐷𝑓(𝑥) =𝑘(𝑥 −𝛼)𝑘−1𝑔(𝑥) +(𝑥 −𝛼)𝑘𝐷𝑔(𝑥)Df(x)=k(x−α)k−1g(x)+(x−α)kDg(x) necessarily also has root 𝛼α. Conversely, if 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) and 𝐷𝑓(𝑥)Df(x) both have root 𝛼α, then for the splitting 𝑓(𝑥) =(𝑥 −𝛼)𝑔(𝑥)f(x)=(x−α)g(x), we have 𝐷𝑓(𝑥) =(𝑥 −𝛼)𝐷𝑔(𝑥) +𝑔(𝑥)Df(x)=(x−α)Dg(x)+g(x), so 𝛼α is also a root of 𝑔(𝑥)g(x), hence 𝛼α is a multiple root of 𝑓(𝑥)f(x). This proves the first part of the theorem. Furthermore, 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) has a multiple root 𝛼α if and only if 𝑥 −𝛼x−α is a factor of gcd(𝑓(𝑥),𝐷𝑓(𝑥))gcd(f(x),Df(x)). So 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) is inseparable is equivalent to deg⁡gcd(𝑓(𝑥),𝐷𝑓(𝑥)) ≥1deg⁡gcd(f(x),Df(x))≥1.

    Polynomials over fields can always be factored into products of irreducible polynomials. Because (up to associates) different irreducible polynomials always have different roots, repeated roots naturally link to repeated polynomial factors. Then, if there are no repeated irreducible factors in the factorization, can we determine that the polynomial is separable? In other words, are all irreducible polynomials separable? Unfortunately, in general, we cannot get a positive answer. The problem arises with fields of finite characteristic.

    For an irreducible polynomial 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) over a field 𝐹F, gcd(𝑓(𝑥),𝐷𝑓(𝑥))gcd(f(x),Df(x)) as a factor of 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) can only be either 11 or 𝑓(𝑥)f(x). In the first case, 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) is naturally separable; the problem is in the second case. However, since the definition of the derivative already guarantees 𝐷𝑓(𝑥) =0Df(x)=0 or deg⁡𝐷𝑓(𝑥) <deg⁡𝑓(𝑥)deg⁡Df(x)<deg⁡f(x), that 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) becomes a factor of 𝐷𝑓(𝑥)Df(x) can only mean 𝐷𝑓(𝑥) =0Df(x)=0. This is possible in fields of finite characteristic.

    For a field 𝐹F of characteristic 𝑝p, if 𝐷𝑓(𝑥) =0Df(x)=0, then all non-zero coefficients of the polynomial can only appear in terms whose degrees are multiples of exactly 𝑝p, that is, the polynomial 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) can be written as

    𝑓(𝑥)=𝑎0+𝑎𝑝𝑥𝑝+𝑎2𝑝𝑥2𝑝+⋯+𝑎(𝑘−1)𝑝𝑥(𝑘−1)𝑝+𝑎𝑘𝑝𝑥𝑘𝑝.f(x)=a0+apxp+a2px2p+⋯+a(k−1)px(k−1)p+akpxkp.

    If there really exists an irreducible polynomial 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) over 𝐹F that is both irreducible and inseparable, it can only have this form. However, if all elements in 𝐹F always have 𝑝p-th roots, that is, for each coefficient 𝑎𝑗𝑝ajp there exists 𝑏𝑗 ∈𝐹bj∈F such that 𝑎𝑗𝑝ajp can be written as 𝑏𝑝𝑗bjp, then by the Frobenius endomorphism, we always have

    𝑓(𝑥)=𝑎0+𝑎𝑝𝑥𝑝+𝑎2𝑝𝑥2𝑝+⋯+𝑎(𝑘−1)𝑝𝑥(𝑘−1)𝑝+𝑎𝑘𝑝𝑥𝑘𝑝=𝑏𝑝0+𝑏𝑝1𝑥𝑝+𝑏𝑝2𝑥2𝑝+⋯+𝑏𝑝𝑘−1𝑥(𝑘−1)𝑝+𝑏𝑝𝑘𝑥𝑘𝑝=(𝑏0+𝑏1𝑥+𝑏2𝑥+⋯+𝑏𝑘−1𝑥𝑘−1+𝑏𝑘𝑥𝑘)𝑝.f(x)=a0+apxp+a2px2p+⋯+a(k−1)px(k−1)p+akpxkp=b0p+b1pxp+b2px2p+⋯+bk−1px(k−1)p+bkpxkp=(b0+b1x+b2x+⋯+bk−1xk−1+bkxk)p.

    Therefore, such irreducible polynomials do not exist on such fields 𝐹F. Thus, on such fields, all irreducible polynomials are separable. Such fields are called perfect fields.

    Perfect Field

    If all irreducible polynomials over a field 𝐹F are separable, then 𝐹F is called a perfect field.

    For perfect fields, the concept of separable polynomials is equivalent to the concept of polynomials with no square factors in their factorization.

    Theorem

    Let 𝐹F be a perfect field. Then a polynomial over 𝐹F is separable if and only if it can be written as a product of (up to associates) distinct irreducible polynomials.

    The discussion in this section is actually sufficient to provide a method for removing repeated factors in polynomials, which is a key step in polynomial factorization algorithms. But this is beyond the scope of this article. Interested readers can refer to related materials at the end of this article.

    This discussion actually also gives a characterization of perfect fields:

    Theorem

    A field 𝐹F is perfect if and only if either the characteristic of 𝐹F is zero, or the characteristic of 𝐹F is 𝑝p and every element 𝑥 ∈𝐹x∈F has a 𝑝p-th root (that is, the Frobenius endomorphism is also an automorphism).

    The rational field 𝐐Q and the finite fields 𝐅𝑞Fq discussed below are all perfect fields.

    For fields that are not perfect fields, there do exist inseparable irreducible polynomials.

    Examples

    Consider the polynomial 𝑥2 −𝑡x2−t over the rational function field 𝐅2(𝑡)F2(t) of 𝐅2F2. Since 𝐅2(𝑡)F2(t) is the fraction field of the unique factorization domain 𝐅2[𝑡]F2[t], and 𝑡t is a prime element in 𝐅2[𝑡]F2[t], applying the Eisenstein criterion to the prime element 𝑡t shows that 𝑥2 −𝑡x2−t is irreducible in 𝐅2[𝑡]F2[t], hence it is also irreducible in 𝐅2(𝑡)F2(t). However, its derivative is 00, so 𝑥2 −𝑡x2−t is not separable. In fact, in the extension field 𝐅2(𝑡)(√𝑡)F2(t)(t), it has the double root √𝑡t.

    Finally, we return to the discussion of field extensions.

    Separable Extension

    For an algebraic extension 𝐸/𝐹E/F, if the minimal polynomial of every 𝛼 ∈𝐸α∈E is a separable polynomial, then 𝐸E is called a separable extension of 𝐹F.

    All algebraic extensions over perfect fields are separable extensions. This can also serve as an equivalent definition of perfect fields.

    If an algebraic extension is both a normal extension and a separable extension, it is also called a Galois extension. In Galois extensions, no irreducible polynomial has multiple roots, and the number of roots is always exactly equal to the degree of the polynomial. Thus, permutations of roots can fully reflect the properties of field extensions and polynomials. Such extensions provide the cornerstone for establishing Galois theory. Interested readers can refer to related materials at the end of this article.

    Cyclotomic Fields

    As a simple example of field extensions, this section discusses cyclotomic fields. Another simple example of field extensions is Quadratic Fields.

    Group of Roots of Unity

    In the complex field 𝐂C, the roots of the polynomial 𝑥𝑛 =1xn=1 are called 𝑛n-th roots of unity. Let 𝜁𝑛 =e2𝜋i/𝑛ζn=e2πi/n. Then all 𝑛n-th roots of unity are the set 𝐶𝑛 ={𝜁𝑘𝑛 :𝑘 ∈𝐙}Cn={ζnk:k∈Z}. Under multiplication, 𝐶𝑛Cn forms a cyclic group of order 𝑛n, which can be denoted ⟨𝜁𝑛⟩⟨ζn⟩, and is called the group of 𝑛n-th roots of unity. The generators of the group 𝐶𝑛Cn, that is, elements with order exactly 𝑛n, are called primitive 𝑛n-th roots of unity. The set of 𝑛n-th primitive roots of unity is 𝑃𝑛 =𝜁𝑘𝑛:𝑘∈𝐙,𝑘⟂𝑛Pn=ζnk:k∈Z,k⟂n, which has exactly 𝜑(𝑛)φ(n) elements; here, 𝜑(𝑛)φ(n) is the Euler function. Classifying the elements of the root of unity group 𝐶𝑛Cn by their orders gives the following decomposition:

    𝐶𝑛=⋃𝑑|𝑛𝑃𝑑.Cn=⋃d|nPd.

    Counting elements on both sides gives the identity 𝑛 =∑𝑑∣𝑛𝜑(𝑑)n=∑d∣nφ(d).

    Cyclotomic Fields

    The cyclotomic field is the extension field obtained by adding roots of unity to the rational field.

    Cyclotomic Field

    The extension field 𝐐(𝜁𝑛)Q(ζn) obtained by adding the 𝑛n-th complex root of unity 𝜁𝑛 =e2𝜋i/𝑛ζn=e2πi/n to the rational field 𝐐Q is called the 𝑛n-th cyclotomic field.

    Since all 𝑛n-th roots of unity form a cyclic group ⟨𝜁𝑛⟩⟨ζn⟩ under multiplication, the cyclotomic field 𝐐(𝜁𝑛)Q(ζn) also includes all these 𝑛n-th roots of unity. In fact, 𝐐(𝜁𝑛)Q(ζn) is precisely the splitting field of the polynomial 𝑥𝑛 −1xn−1 over 𝐐Q.

    Theorem

    The cyclotomic field 𝐐(𝜁𝑛)Q(ζn) is the splitting field of the polynomial 𝑥𝑛 −1xn−1 over 𝐐Q.

    Proof

    Let 𝐹F be the splitting field of 𝑥𝑛 −1xn−1 over 𝐐Q. Since 𝐐(𝜁𝑛)Q(ζn) contains all complex roots of 𝑥𝑛 −1xn−1, we have 𝐹 ⊆𝐐(𝜁𝑛)F⊆Q(ζn). Conversely, since 𝜁𝑛 ∈𝐹ζn∈F, we must have 𝐐(𝜁𝑛) =𝐹Q(ζn)=F. This shows that 𝐹 =𝐐(𝜁𝑛)F=Q(ζn).

    This can serve as an equivalent definition of cyclotomic fields. In fact, adding any 𝑛n-th primitive root of unity to the cyclotomic field yields 𝐐(𝜁𝑛)Q(ζn).

    Cyclotomic Polynomials

    The cyclotomic field 𝐐(𝜁𝑛)Q(ζn) is a simple algebraic extension over 𝐐Q. According to the analysis above, such fields are always isomorphic to the quotient ring of some polynomial ring. To obtain such an isomorphism, we need to analyze the minimal polynomial 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) of 𝜁𝑛ζn. Since 𝜁𝑛ζn is a root of 𝑥𝑛 −1xn−1, 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) must be a factor of 𝑥𝑛 −1xn−1. This shows that we need to examine the factorization of 𝑥𝑛 −1xn−1 in 𝐐[𝑥]Q[x]. According to Gauss's Lemma, it can be factored in 𝐙[𝑥]Z[x] as a product of several irreducible monic polynomials.

    Since 𝐐(𝜁𝑛)Q(ζn) is a splitting field, 𝑥𝑛 −1xn−1 factors as:

    𝑥𝑛−1=∏𝜁∈𝐶𝑛(𝑥−𝜁)=∏𝑑∣𝑛∏𝜁∈𝑃𝑑(𝑥−𝜁).xn−1=∏ζ∈Cn(x−ζ)=∏d∣n∏ζ∈Pd(x−ζ).

    Because roots of unity with different orders have different algebraic properties, they cannot be roots of the same irreducible polynomial. Therefore, to examine the minimal polynomial of 𝜁𝑛ζn, we only need to consider the factor

    Φ𝑛(𝑥)=∏𝜁∈𝑃𝑛(𝑥−𝜁)Φn(x)=∏ζ∈Pn(x−ζ)

    in the above decomposition. The minimal polynomial of 𝜁𝑛ζn must be a factor of Φ𝑛(𝑥)Φn(x). Moreover, Φ𝑛(𝑥)Φn(x) defined this way has the following properties:

    Theorem

    Φ𝑛(𝑥)Φn(x) is a monic polynomial with integer coefficients, and is irreducible in 𝐙[𝑥]Z[x].

    Proof

    By definition, Φ𝑛(𝑥)Φn(x) is obviously a monic polynomial. First, prove Φ𝑛(𝑥) ∈𝐙[𝑥]Φn(x)∈Z[x]. According to Gauss's Lemma, 𝑥𝑛 −1xn−1 has the same factorization in 𝐙[𝑥]Z[x] and 𝐐[𝑥]Q[x], and each factor is a monic polynomial with integer coefficients. In this factorization, each factor 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) is irreducible over 𝐐[𝑥]Q[x] and splits in 𝐐(𝜁𝑛)Q(ζn); all its roots are 𝑛n-th roots of unity and necessarily have the same order, so these roots all belong to some 𝑃𝑑Pd rather than existing in different 𝑃𝑑Pd's. This means that each 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) is a factor of some Φ𝑑(𝑥)Φd(x). Therefore, Φ𝑛(𝑥)Φn(x) can be written as a product of several monic polynomials with integer coefficients, so it is also a monic polynomial with integer coefficients.

    Next, prove Φ𝑛(𝑥)Φn(x) is irreducible in 𝐙[𝑥]Z[x]. Suppose it factors as 𝑓(𝑥)𝑔(𝑥)f(x)g(x) with 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) irreducible in 𝐙[𝑥]Z[x]. We only need to prove 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) contains all 𝑛n-th primitive roots of unity. That is, let 𝜁ζ be a root of 𝑓(𝑥)f(x), and we need to prove that for all 𝑘 ⟂𝑛k⟂n, 𝜁𝑘ζk is also a root of 𝑓(𝑥)f(x); since 𝑘k can always be decomposed into prime factors, we only need to prove that for all primes 𝑝 ⟂𝑛p⟂n, 𝜁𝑝ζp is a root of 𝑓(𝑥)f(x). Assume the contrary, 𝜁𝑝ζp is a root of 𝑔(𝑥)g(x). Therefore, 𝜁ζ is a common root of 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) and 𝑔(𝑥𝑝)g(xp) in 𝐙[𝑥]Z[x]. Because 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) is the minimal polynomial of 𝜁ζ over 𝐐Q, 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) must divide 𝑔(𝑥𝑝)g(xp); that is, there exists ℎ(𝑥) ∈𝐙[𝑥]h(x)∈Z[x] such that 𝑔(𝑥𝑝) =𝑓(𝑥)ℎ(𝑥)g(xp)=f(x)h(x). Taking modulo 𝑝p on both sides of the equation gives ――𝑔(𝑥𝑝) =――𝑓(𝑥)――ℎ(𝑥)g―(xp)=f―(x)h―(x) over 𝐅𝑝[𝑥]Fp[x]. Using the Frobenius endomorphism, ――𝑔(𝑥)𝑝 =――𝑓(𝑥)――ℎ(𝑥)g―(x)p=f―(x)h―(x). Since 𝐅𝑝[𝑥]Fp[x] is also a unique factorization domain, ――𝑔(𝑥)g―(x) and ――𝑓(𝑥)f―(x) must have a non-trivial common factor, so 𝑥𝑛 −――1 =――𝑓(𝑥)――𝑔(𝑥)xn−1―=f―(x)g―(x) is inseparable over 𝐅𝑝Fp. However, since 𝑝 ⟂𝑛p⟂n, its formal derivative 𝑛𝑥𝑛−1nxn−1 is coprime with itself, which contradicts its inseparability. Therefore, 𝜁𝑝ζp must be a root of 𝑓(𝑥)f(x), so 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) contains all 𝑛n-th primitive roots of unity, and it is Φ𝑛(𝑥)Φn(x).

    This shows that it is the minimal polynomial of 𝜁𝑛ζn, also called the 𝑛n-th cyclotomic polynomial. The definition above shows that it has 𝜑(𝑛)φ(n) complex roots, and these complex roots are precisely all 𝑛n-th primitive roots of unity; here, 𝜑(𝑛)φ(n) is the Euler function. This also shows that 𝐐(𝜁𝑛)/𝐐Q(ζn)/Q is an extension of degree 𝜑(𝑛)φ(n).

    The ring of algebraic integers in the cyclotomic field 𝐐(𝜁𝑛)Q(ζn) is 𝐙[𝜁𝑛]Z[ζn]. Additionally, when 𝜑(𝑛) =2φ(n)=2, the cyclotomic field is a quadratic extension. Specifically, 𝐐(𝜁4)Q(ζ4) is the quadratic field 𝐐(√−1)Q(−1); 𝐐(𝜁3)Q(ζ3) and 𝐐(𝜁6)Q(ζ6) are the same, both being the quadratic field 𝐐(√−3)Q(−3).

    Using cyclotomic polynomials, 𝑥𝑛 −1xn−1 has a unique factorization in 𝐙[𝑥]Z[x]

    𝑥𝑛−1=∏𝑑∣𝑛Φ𝑑(𝑥).xn−1=∏d∣nΦd(x).

    Therefore, (𝑥𝑑 −1) ∣(𝑥𝑛 −1)(xd−1)∣(xn−1) if and only if 𝑑 ∣𝑛d∣n. Moreover, applying Möbius inversion to this formula gives

    Φ𝑑(𝑥)=∏𝑑∣𝑛(𝑥𝑑−1)𝜇(𝑛/𝑑).Φd(x)=∏d∣n(xd−1)μ(n/d).

    Using this expression, we can recursively compute all cyclotomic polynomials. Here are examples of the first few cyclotomic polynomials for readers to become familiar with.

    Cyclotomic Polynomials

    The first 10 cyclotomic polynomials are as follows:

    Φ1(𝑥)=𝑥−1,Φ2(𝑥)=𝑥+1,Φ3(𝑥)=𝑥2+𝑥+1,Φ4(𝑥)=𝑥2+1,Φ5(𝑥)=𝑥4+𝑥3+𝑥2+𝑥+1,Φ6(𝑥)=𝑥2−𝑥+1,Φ7(𝑥)=𝑥6+𝑥5+𝑥4+𝑥3+𝑥2+𝑥+1,Φ8(𝑥)=𝑥4+1,Φ9(𝑥)=𝑥6+𝑥3+1,Φ10(𝑥)=𝑥4−𝑥3+𝑥2−𝑥+1.Φ1(x)=x−1,Φ2(x)=x+1,Φ3(x)=x2+x+1,Φ4(x)=x2+1,Φ5(x)=x4+x3+x2+x+1,Φ6(x)=x2−x+1,Φ7(x)=x6+x5+x4+x3+x2+x+1,Φ8(x)=x4+1,Φ9(x)=x6+x3+1,Φ10(x)=x4−x3+x2−x+1.

    An interesting fact is that although it appears that the coefficients of these cyclotomic polynomials can only be 00 and ±1±1, this conclusion is not true for general 𝑛n. The first counterexample appears in Φ105(𝑥)Φ105(x), and it can be proven that as 𝑛n increases, the coefficients can take arbitrarily large values.

    Using the Möbius inversion formula above, we can summarize the following properties to simplify the computation of Φ𝑛(𝑥)Φn(x):

    Properties

    For the cyclotomic polynomial Φ𝑛(𝑥)Φn(x), we have:

    1. If a prime 𝑝 ∣𝑛p∣n, then Φ𝑝𝑛(𝑥) =Φ𝑛(𝑥𝑝)Φpn(x)=Φn(xp);
    2. If a prime 𝑝 ⟂𝑛p⟂n, then Φ𝑝𝑛(𝑥) =Φ𝑛(𝑥𝑝)Φ𝑛(𝑥)Φpn(x)=Φn(xp)Φn(x);
    3. Specifically, if 𝑛n is odd, then Φ2𝑛(𝑥) =Φ𝑛( −𝑥)Φ2n(x)=Φn(−x);
    4. For a prime 𝑝p, Φ𝑝(𝑥) =1 +𝑥 +⋯ +𝑥𝑝−1Φp(x)=1+x+⋯+xp−1;
    5. Specifically, Φ2𝑘(𝑥) =𝑥2𝑘−1 +1Φ2k(x)=x2k−1+1.

    These properties show that the computation of cyclotomic polynomials focuses on the case where the degree is a square-free odd number. And for such cases, we can add prime factors one by one using property 2; each addition of a prime factor only requires one polynomial division.

    Cyclotomic polynomials have many other properties.

    Theorem

    Let Φ𝑛(𝑥)Φn(x) be the 𝑛 >1n>1-th cyclotomic polynomial, and the degree of the polynomial is 𝜑(𝑛)φ(n). Then we have:

    1. Φ𝑛(𝑥)Φn(x) is a palindromic polynomial, its 𝑗j-th coefficient and 𝜑(𝑛) −𝑗φ(n)−j-th coefficient are the same, that is, Φ𝑛(𝑥) =𝑥𝜑(𝑛)Φ𝑛(1/𝑥)Φn(x)=xφ(n)Φn(1/x);
    2. The coefficient of the 𝜑(𝑛) −1φ(n)−1-th term equals −𝜇(𝑛)−μ(n);
    3. If 𝑛n is a prime power 𝑝𝑘pk, then Φ𝑛(1) =𝑝Φn(1)=p; otherwise, Φ𝑛(1) =1Φn(1)=1;
    4. Let 𝑏 >1b>1 and 𝑝p be a prime factor of Φ𝑛(𝑏)Φn(b). Then either 𝑝 ∣𝑛p∣n, or 𝑛n is the order of 𝑏b in the multiplicative group (𝐙/𝑝𝐙)×(Z/pZ)×, and these two cases cannot occur simultaneously.
    Proof

    For the first three properties, we only need to use Möbius inversion. For 1, directly examine the Möbius inversion form of Φ𝑛(𝑥)Φn(x), that is, Φ𝑑(𝑥) =∏𝑑∣𝑛(𝑥𝑑 −1)𝜇(𝑛/𝑑)Φd(x)=∏d∣n(xd−1)μ(n/d); for 2, let the coefficient of the 𝜑(𝑛) −1φ(n)−1-th term of Φ𝑛(𝑥)Φn(x) be 𝑓(𝑛)f(n), then comparing the coefficients of the 𝑛 −1n−1-th term on both sides of 𝑥𝑛 −1 =∏𝑑∣𝑛Φ𝑑(𝑥)xn−1=∏d∣nΦd(x) gives ∑𝑑∣𝑛𝑓(𝑑) = −[𝑛 =1]∑d∣nf(d)=−[n=1], then apply Möbius inversion; for 3, divide both sides of 𝑥𝑛 −1 =∏𝑑∣𝑛Φ𝑛(𝑥)xn−1=∏d∣nΦn(x) by Φ1(𝑥) =𝑥 −1Φ1(x)=x−1, then substitute 𝑥 =1x=1, giving 𝑛 =∏𝑑∣𝑛,𝑑≠1Φ𝑛(1)n=∏d∣n,d≠1Φn(1), then apply Möbius inversion.

    Now prove the fourth property. First, if 𝑛n is the order of 𝑏b in the multiplicative group (𝐙/𝑝𝐙)×(Z/pZ)×, then 𝑛n is the smallest positive integer satisfying 𝑝 ∣𝑏𝑛 −1p∣bn−1, so 𝑝 ∣Φ𝑛(𝑏)p∣Φn(b). Conversely, if 𝑝 ∣Φ𝑛(𝑏)p∣Φn(b), then 𝑏𝑛 ≡1(mod𝑝)bn≡1(modp); but if 𝑛n is not the order of 𝑏b in the multiplicative group (𝐙/𝑝𝐙)×(Z/pZ)×, then let its order be 𝑘k, we must have 𝑘 ∣𝑛k∣n and 𝑝 ∣Φ𝑘(𝑏)p∣Φk(b). At this time, Φ𝑘(𝑥)Φk(x) and Φ𝑛(𝑥)Φn(x) have a common root 𝑏b in 𝐅𝑝Fp, which shows that 𝑥𝑛 −1xn−1 has a multiple root 𝑏b. This shows that 𝑝 ∣𝑛p∣n; otherwise, 𝑥𝑛 −1xn−1 is coprime with its derivative, so it is separable over 𝐅𝑝Fp and cannot have multiple roots. Therefore, the prime factors of Φ𝑛(𝑏)Φn(b) have only two cases: 𝑝 ∣𝑛p∣n, or 𝑛n is the order of 𝑏b in (𝐙/𝑝𝐙)×(Z/pZ)×. These two cases are mutually exclusive, because the latter means 𝑛 ∣𝑝 −1n∣p−1.

    Cyclotomic polynomials can also solve some number theory and algebra problems. For example, the length of the repeating part of a decimal in a certain base is closely related to cyclotomic polynomials. For these specific applications, interested readers can refer to the materials at the end of this article.

    Finite Fields

    A finite field, also called a Galois field, is a field with only finitely many elements. The structure of a finite field is uniquely determined by its number of elements, and the number of elements must be a power of a prime.

    Theorem

    A field of size 𝑞q exists if and only if 𝑞q has the form of a prime power 𝑝𝑛pn. Moreover, such a field is unique up to isomorphism, denoted 𝐅𝑞Fq. The prime 𝑝p is the characteristic of 𝐅𝑞Fq, and the positive integer 𝑛n is the degree of the extension 𝐅𝑞/𝐅𝑝Fq/Fp. Finally, 𝐅𝑞Fq is the splitting field of the polynomial 𝑥𝑞 −𝑥xq−x over 𝐅𝑝Fp, and it contains exactly 𝑞q distinct roots of 𝑥𝑞 −𝑥xq−x.

    Proof

    Let 𝐹F be a finite field. The characteristic of 𝐹F is necessarily finite, denoted 𝑝p; therefore, 𝐹F has the prime subfield 𝐅𝑝Fp. Moreover, 𝐹F is necessarily a finite extension of 𝐅𝑝Fp, with the degree of extension denoted 𝑛n. As an 𝑛n-dimensional vector space over 𝐅𝑝Fp, 𝐹F has 𝑞 =𝑝𝑛q=pn elements. The set of all non-zero elements of 𝐹F forms the group 𝐹×F× of order 𝑞 −1q−1, so 𝑥𝑞−1 =1xq−1=1. Therefore, 𝐹 =𝐹× ∪{0}F=F×∪{0} satisfies 𝑥𝑞 =𝑥xq=x, i.e., they are the 𝑞q distinct roots of 𝑥𝑞 −𝑥xq−x. Therefore, in 𝐹F, 𝑥𝑞 −𝑥xq−x has the factor ∏𝛼∈𝐹(𝑥 −𝛼)∏α∈F(x−α), but the degree of this factor is already 𝑞q and the leading coefficient is 11, so 𝑥𝑞 −𝑥 =∏𝛼∈𝐹(𝑥 −𝛼)xq−x=∏α∈F(x−α). This shows that 𝑥𝑞 −𝑥xq−x splits in 𝐹F. For any field that can make 𝑥𝑞 −𝑥xq−x split, since 𝑥𝑞 −𝑥xq−x has 𝑞q distinct roots, there must be at least 𝑞q elements. This shows that 𝐹F is the smallest field making 𝑥𝑞 −𝑥xq−x split, i.e., the splitting field of 𝑥𝑞 −𝑥xq−x. In summary, a finite field of size 𝑞q is necessarily the splitting field of 𝑥𝑞 −𝑥xq−x over its prime subfield. Since splitting fields are unique up to isomorphism, fields of size 𝑞q are also unique.

    Conversely, given a prime 𝑝p and its power 𝑞 =𝑝𝑛q=pn, to show that the splitting field of 𝑥𝑞 −𝑥xq−x over 𝐅𝑝Fp has exactly 𝑞q elements, we can only prove that all fields of order 𝑞q exist. Since the splitting field of 𝑥𝑞 −𝑥xq−x over 𝐅𝑝Fp always exists, let 𝐹F be the set of all roots of 𝑥𝑞 −𝑥xq−x in this splitting field. Now we need to prove that 𝐹F is a field, so it is itself the splitting field of 𝑥𝑞 −𝑥xq−x. However, iterating the Frobenius endomorphism 𝑛n times shows that 𝑥 ↦𝑥𝑞x↦xq is also an endomorphism, so for any 𝛼,𝛽 ∈𝐹α,β∈F, we have (𝛼 ±𝛽)𝑞 =𝛼𝑞 ±𝛽𝑞(α±β)q=αq±βq, (𝛼𝛽)𝑞 =𝛼𝑞𝛽𝑞(αβ)q=αqβq and (𝛼−1)𝑞 =(𝛼𝑞)−1(α−1)q=(αq)−1. Therefore, the set 𝐹F is closed under addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division, it is a field. This shows that 𝐹F is the splitting field of 𝑥𝑞 −𝑥xq−x over 𝐅𝑝Fp.

    Corollary

    In a finite field 𝐅𝑞Fq (𝑞 >2q>2), the sum of all non-zero elements is 00, and the product is −1−1.

    Proof

    The non-zero elements of a finite field are exactly the 𝑞 −1q−1 distinct roots of 𝑥𝑞−1 −1xq−1−1, and applying Vieta's theorem gives the result.

    In the prime field 𝐅𝑝Fp, the conclusion about the product in this corollary is precisely part of Wilson's Theorem in number theory.

    Multiplicative Structure

    The multiplicative group 𝐅× =𝐅 ∖{0}F×=F∖{0} of a finite field is always a cyclic group.

    Theorem

    Any finite subgroup of the multiplicative group of a field is always cyclic.

    Proof

    Let 𝐺G be a subgroup of the multiplicative group of 𝐹F with |𝐺| =𝑛|G|=n. Then 𝐺G is a finite abelian group. According to the fundamental theorem of finite abelian groups, 𝐺G has invariant factor decomposition 𝐶𝑛1 ×⋯ ×𝐶𝑛𝑠Cn1×⋯×Cns with 𝑛1 ∣⋯ ∣𝑛𝑠n1∣⋯∣ns. So for all elements 𝑥x in 𝐺G, 𝑥𝑛𝑠 =1xns=1. That is, all elements of 𝐺G are roots of the polynomial 𝑥𝑛𝑠 −1xns−1 over 𝐹F. But 𝑥𝑛𝑠 −1xns−1 has at most 𝑛𝑠ns distinct roots, i.e., 𝑛 ≤𝑛𝑠n≤ns. But 𝑛𝑠 ≤𝑛ns≤n, so 𝑛𝑠 =𝑛ns=n. This shows 𝐺 ≅𝐶𝑛𝑠G≅Cns, i.e., 𝐺G is cyclic.

    Corollary

    The multiplicative group of a finite field 𝐅𝑞Fq is 𝐅×𝑞 ≅𝐶𝑞−1Fq×≅Cq−1.

    In the cyclic group 𝐅×𝑞Fq×, there are 𝜑(𝑞 −1)φ(q−1) generators, which are called primitive elements of the finite field; here, 𝜑(𝑛)φ(n) is the Euler function.

    Primitive Element

    A generator of the multiplicative group of a finite field 𝐅𝑞Fq is called a primitive element of 𝐅𝑞Fq.

    Primitive Elements in Simple Extensions and Finite Fields are Different

    Although the names are the same, primitive elements in simple extensions and primitive elements in finite fields are different. Primitive elements in simple extensions are generators of the corresponding simple extension, while primitive elements in finite fields are generators of the corresponding multiplicative group (as a cyclic group). The primitive element of a finite field as a simple extension of its prime subfield is not necessarily a primitive element of the finite field itself. For example, in 𝐅25 ≅𝐅5[𝑥]/(𝑥2 +𝑥 +1)F25≅F5[x]/(x2+x+1), ――𝑥x― is a primitive element of the field extension, but not a primitive element of 𝐅25F25 because its order is 33.

    Primitive Elements in 𝐅𝑞Fq and Primitive Roots Modulo 𝑞q are Also Different

    For finite fields 𝐅𝑞Fq of odd characteristic, there always exists a primitive root modulo 𝑞q. However, it should not be confused with primitive elements (primitive elements) in finite fields 𝐅𝑞Fq. Although they are both generators of the corresponding multiplicative structure as a cyclic group, (𝐙/𝑞𝐙)×(Z/qZ)× and 𝐅𝑞Fq are not the same when 𝑞q itself is not prime. For example, the order of the former is 𝜑(𝑞)φ(q) while the order of the latter is 𝑞 −1q−1, so the sizes of the two multiplicative groups are not the same.

    Let 𝛼α be a primitive element of a finite field 𝐅𝑞Fq. Then for all 𝑥 ∈𝐅𝑞x∈Fq, there exists a unique natural number 𝑘 <𝑞 −1k<q−1 such that 𝑥 =𝛼𝑘x=αk; this 𝑘k is called the discrete logarithm of 𝑥x over 𝐅𝑞Fq with respect to the basis 𝛼α. Consistent with the case over 𝐅𝑝Fp, the complexity of discrete logarithm algorithms is relatively high.

    Through multiplication, primitive elements can generate all non-zero elements of the field. This shows that a finite field, as an extension of its subfield, is necessarily a simple extension.

    Theorem

    For a finite field 𝐅𝑞Fq, let 𝐹F be a subfield of 𝐅𝑞Fq. Then 𝐅𝑞Fq is a simple algebraic extension over 𝐹F; also let 𝛼α be a primitive element of 𝐅𝑞Fq, then 𝐅𝑞 =𝐹(𝛼)Fq=F(α).

    The minimal polynomial of a primitive element is an irreducible polynomial over a subfield of the finite field.

    Containment Relations

    Subfields of finite fields are also finite fields. The containment relations between finite fields are also completely determined by their orders.

    Theorem

    Let 𝐅𝑞Fq and 𝐅𝑟Fr be finite fields. Then 𝐅𝑟Fr is a subfield of 𝐅𝑞Fq if and only if there exists 𝑘k such that 𝑞 =𝑟𝑘q=rk. In other words, 𝐅𝑝𝑑Fpd is a subfield of 𝐅𝑝𝑛Fpn if and only if 𝑑 ∣𝑛d∣n.

    Proof

    If 𝐅𝑟Fr is a subfield of 𝐅𝑞Fq, they must have the same characteristic 𝑝p. The field extensions 𝐅𝑞/𝐅𝑟Fq/Fr, 𝐅𝑟/𝐅𝑝Fr/Fp, and 𝐅𝑞/𝐅𝑝Fq/Fp are all simple algebraic extensions, with degrees 𝑘k, 𝑑d, and 𝑛n respectively, and the degrees satisfy 𝑛 =𝑘𝑑n=kd. Moreover, 𝑟 =𝑝𝑑r=pd and 𝑞 =𝑝𝑛q=pn, and 𝑞 =𝑝𝑛 =𝑝𝑘𝑑 =(𝑝𝑑)𝑘 =𝑟𝑘q=pn=pkd=(pd)k=rk.

    Conversely, to prove that for all 𝑑 ∣𝑛d∣n, 𝐅𝑝𝑑Fpd is a subfield of 𝐅𝑝𝑛Fpn. Let 𝑟 =𝑝𝑑r=pd and 𝑞 =𝑝𝑛q=pn. Let 𝐹F be the set of all roots of 𝑥𝑟 −𝑥 =0xr−x=0 in 𝐅𝑞Fq. Through the Frobenius endomorphism, 𝐹F necessarily forms a field; the key is to prove that there are exactly 𝑟r such roots, so 𝐹 ≅𝐅𝑟F≅Fr. Since 𝑑 ∣𝑛d∣n, (𝑝𝑑 −1) ∣(𝑝𝑛 −1)(pd−1)∣(pn−1), so (𝑥𝑝𝑑−1 −1) ∣(𝑥𝑝𝑛−1 −1)(xpd−1−1)∣(xpn−1−1), i.e., (𝑥𝑟 −𝑥) ∣(𝑥𝑞 −𝑥)(xr−x)∣(xq−x). Therefore, 𝑥𝑟 −𝑥xr−x splits over 𝐅𝑞Fq, so there are 𝑟r distinct roots in 𝐅𝑞Fq. This shows that 𝐹 ≅𝐅𝑟F≅Fr is a subfield of 𝐅𝑞Fq.

    This theorem shows that the containment relations between finite fields 𝐅𝑝𝑛Fpn correspond to the divisibility relations between the exponents 𝑛n in the orders 𝑝𝑛pn. The lattice formed by all finite fields 𝐅𝑝𝑛Fpn of characteristic 𝑝p is isomorphic to the lattice formed by integers 𝑛n under divisibility. Of course, to make the intersection and other operations between 𝐅𝑝𝑛Fpn meaningful, we need to embed all fields of characteristic 𝑝p into the algebraic closure of 𝐅𝑝Fp.

    Theorem

    Let 𝐹F be the algebraic closure of 𝐅𝑝Fp. Then the set of roots of 𝑥𝑝𝑛 −𝑥xpn−x in 𝐹F forms the finite field 𝐅𝑝𝑛Fpn. Then we have:

    1. 𝐹 =⋃∞𝑛=1𝐅𝑝𝑛F=⋃n=1∞Fpn, i.e., the algebraic closure of 𝐅𝑝Fp is the union of all finite fields of characteristic 𝑝p;
    2. The lattice formed by all finite fields 𝐅𝑝𝑛Fpn of characteristic 𝑝p under containment is isomorphic to the lattice formed by integers 𝑛n under divisibility. In particular, 𝐅𝑝𝑛 ∩𝐅𝑝𝑚 =𝐅𝑝gcd(𝑛,𝑚)Fpn∩Fpm=Fpgcd(n,m), and the smallest field containing both 𝐅𝑝𝑛Fpn and 𝐅𝑝𝑚Fpm is 𝐅𝑝lcm⁡(𝑛,𝑚)Fplcm⁡(n,m).
    Proof

    The key is to prove the first part, that ⋃∞𝑛=1𝐅𝑝𝑛⋃n=1∞Fpn is the algebraic closure of 𝐅𝑝Fp. The second part is a simple corollary of the theorem about subfields of finite fields.

    Note that for any 𝛼 ∈⋃∞𝑛=1𝐅𝑝𝑛α∈⋃n=1∞Fpn, there exists 𝑛 ∈𝐍+n∈N+ such that 𝛼 ∈𝐅𝑝𝑛α∈Fpn, so 𝛼α is algebraic over 𝐅𝑝Fp; therefore, ⋃∞𝑛=1𝐅𝑝𝑛⋃n=1∞Fpn is an algebraic extension of 𝐅𝑝Fp. For any polynomial 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) of degree 𝑚m over 𝐅𝑝Fp, it has at most 𝑚m distinct roots {𝛼𝑖}𝑚𝑖=1{αi}i=1m in the algebraic closure 𝐹F. Let the degree of the minimal polynomial of 𝛼𝑖αi be 𝑛𝑖ni, then 𝛼𝑖αi is necessarily contained in 𝐅𝑝𝑛𝑖Fpni; therefore, all roots of 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) are in 𝛼 ∈⋃∞𝑛=1𝐅𝑝𝑛α∈⋃n=1∞Fpn, i.e., 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) splits over 𝛼 ∈⋃∞𝑛=1𝐅𝑝𝑛α∈⋃n=1∞Fpn. According to the definition of algebraic closure, 𝛼 ∈⋃∞𝑛=1𝐅𝑝𝑛α∈⋃n=1∞Fpn is the algebraic closure of 𝐅𝑝Fp.

    Automorphism Group

    Subfields of a finite field 𝐅𝑞Fq are all sets of roots of polynomials of the form 𝑥𝑟 −𝑥xr−x. In other words, they are all fixed point sets of some map 𝑥 ↦𝑥𝑟x↦xr. This actually reveals a deep correspondence between subfields of finite fields and subgroups of the automorphism group.

    All fields of characteristic 𝑝p have the Frobenius endomorphism 𝜎𝑝 :𝑥 ↦𝑥𝑝σp:x↦xp. For finite fields 𝐅𝑞Fq, this is also an automorphism; this shows that all finite fields 𝐅𝑞Fq are perfect fields. The automorphism group of 𝐅𝑞Fq is the cyclic group ⟨𝜎𝑝⟩⟨σp⟩ of order 𝑛n, and one generator is the Frobenius endomorphism 𝜎𝑝σp.

    Theorem

    The automorphism group Aut⁡(𝐅𝑞)Aut⁡(Fq) of a finite field 𝐅𝑞Fq is a cyclic group of order 𝑛n, and the generator 𝜎𝑝σp is the Frobenius endomorphism 𝑥 ↦𝑥𝑝x↦xp.

    Proof

    First, the Frobenius endomorphism 𝜎𝑝σp is an automorphism on the finite field 𝐅𝑞Fq because an injection on a finite set must also be a surjection. Therefore, 𝜎𝑝 ∈Aut⁡(𝐅𝑞)σp∈Aut⁡(Fq).

    Then, the order of 𝜎𝑝σp is 𝑛n. This is because for all 𝑥 ∈𝐅𝑞x∈Fq, we have 𝜎𝑛𝑝(𝑥) =𝑥𝑝𝑛 =𝑥σpn(x)=xpn=x, so 𝑥𝑝𝑛xpn is the identity map; and for any 𝑘 <𝑛k<n, 𝜎𝑘𝑝σpk is not the identity map, otherwise all elements of 𝐅𝑞Fq would be roots of 𝑥𝑝𝑘 −𝑥xpk−x, which is impossible.

    Finally, Aut⁡(𝐅𝑞)Aut⁡(Fq) has at most 𝑛n elements. Let 𝛼α be a primitive element of 𝐅𝑞Fq. Then an automorphism 𝜎 ∈Aut⁡(𝐅𝑞)σ∈Aut⁡(Fq) is uniquely determined by its value at 𝛼α, 𝜎(𝛼)σ(α). However, 𝜎σ must map 𝛼α to its conjugate; otherwise, 𝛼α and 𝜎(𝛼)σ(α) are no longer roots of the same minimal polynomial. There are only 𝑛n such conjugates, which shows that Aut⁡(𝐅𝑞)Aut⁡(Fq) also has at most 𝑛n elements.

    Therefore, the 𝑛n elements in Aut⁡(𝐅𝑞)Aut⁡(Fq) are exactly ⟨𝜎𝑝⟩⟨σp⟩. Theorem proved.

    Subgroups of the automorphism group Aut⁡(𝐅𝑞)Aut⁡(Fq) correspond one-to-one with subfields of 𝐅𝑞Fq.

    Theorem

    Let 𝐅𝑞Fq be a finite field, FF its set of all subfields, and GG the set of all subgroups of its automorphism group Aut⁡(𝐅𝑞)Aut⁡(Fq). Then we have:

    1. For 𝐹 ∈FF∈F, let Aut⁡(𝐅𝑞/𝐹)Aut⁡(Fq/F) be the set of automorphisms in Aut⁡(𝐅𝑞)Aut⁡(Fq) that keep 𝐹F unchanged, i.e., Aut⁡(𝐅𝑞/𝐹) ={𝜎 ∈Aut⁡(𝐅𝑞) :∀𝑥 ∈𝐹(𝜎(𝑥) =𝑥)}Aut⁡(Fq/F)={σ∈Aut⁡(Fq):∀x∈F(σ(x)=x)}, then Aut⁡(𝐅𝑞/𝐹) ≤Aut⁡(𝐅𝑞)Aut⁡(Fq/F)≤Aut⁡(Fq);
    2. For 𝐺 ∈GG∈G, let 𝐹𝐺FG be the intersection of the fixed point sets of all automorphisms in 𝐺G, i.e., 𝐹𝐺 ={𝑥 ∈𝐅𝑞 :∀𝜎 ∈𝐺(𝜎(𝑥) =𝑥)}FG={x∈Fq:∀σ∈G(σ(x)=x)}, then 𝐹𝐺FG is a subfield of 𝐅𝑞Fq;
    3. The maps 𝐹 →Aut⁡(𝐅𝑞/𝐹)F→Aut⁡(Fq/F) and 𝐺 →𝐹𝐺G→FG are inverses of each other, and are a one-to-one correspondence between FF and GG;
    4. This one-to-one correspondence maps containment relations between subfields to containment relations between subgroups, i.e., for any 𝐹1 ⊆𝐹2F1⊆F2, we have Aut⁡(𝐅𝑞/𝐹2) ≤Aut⁡(𝐅𝑞/𝐹1)Aut⁡(Fq/F2)≤Aut⁡(Fq/F1).

    This conclusion is a special case of the fundamental theorem of general Galois theory, connecting field extensions with group theory, thus allowing group theory methods to solve field extension problems.

    Irreducible Polynomials

    Irreducible polynomials over finite fields 𝐅𝑞Fq are very easy to determine. Because each 𝑛n-degree irreducible polynomial over 𝐅𝑞Fq corresponds to an 𝑛n-degree algebraic extension, and such extensions are unique. Therefore, all 𝑛n-degree irreducible polynomial roots can be found in 𝐅𝑞𝑛Fqn. This shows that 𝑛n-degree irreducible polynomials over 𝐅𝑞Fq must be factors of 𝑥𝑞𝑛 −𝑥xqn−x. To determine all 𝑛n-degree irreducible polynomials over 𝐅𝑞Fq, we need to examine the factorization of 𝑥𝑞𝑛 −𝑥xqn−x over 𝐅𝑞Fq. This is very similar to the case of cyclotomic polynomials.

    Algebraic elements over 𝐅𝑞Fq can be classified according to the degree of their minimal polynomials. Let 𝑃𝑛Pn be the set of algebraic elements whose minimal polynomial has degree exactly 𝑛n, then

    𝐅𝑞𝑛=⋃𝑑∣𝑛𝑃𝑑.Fqn=⋃d∣nPd.

    This corresponds to the factorization

    𝑥𝑞𝑛−𝑥=∏𝑑|𝑛∏𝜁∈𝑃𝑑(𝑥−𝜁).xqn−x=∏d|n∏ζ∈Pd(x−ζ).

    Because 𝑛n-degree irreducible polynomials have 𝑛n roots, and all these roots have minimal polynomial degree 𝑛n, 𝑛n-degree irreducible polynomials must be factors of

    ∏𝜁∈𝑃𝑛(𝑥−𝜁)=∏𝑑∣𝑛(𝑥𝑞𝑑−𝑥)𝜇(𝑛/𝑑)∏ζ∈Pn(x−ζ)=∏d∣n(xqd−x)μ(n/d)

    ; this expression is obtained by applying Möbius inversion to the previous factorization. Since the degree of this polynomial is

    ∑𝑑∣𝑛𝜇(𝑑)𝑞𝑛/𝑑,∑d∣nμ(d)qn/d,

    the number of 𝑛n-degree monic irreducible polynomials over 𝐅𝑞Fq is

    1𝑛∑𝑑∣𝑛𝜇(𝑑)𝑞𝑛/𝑑1n∑d∣nμ(d)qn/d

    . This is exactly the number of necklaces of length 𝑛n that can be made with 𝑞q colors (not considering rotations) (proof), so it is also called the necklace polynomial.

    Theorem

    There exist irreducible polynomials of any degree over finite fields 𝐅𝑞Fq.

    Because irreducible polynomials over finite fields have simple structure, factoring polynomials over finite fields is very easy. For example, to determine all 𝑛n-degree irreducible factors of a given polynomial, we only need to find the greatest common divisor of the given polynomial with 𝑥𝑞𝑛 −𝑥xqn−x5. Similarly, if an 𝑛n-degree polynomial is coprime with 𝑥𝑞𝑘 −1xqk−1 for all 𝑘 <𝑛k<n, then we can conclude that the 𝑛n-degree polynomial is irreducible over 𝐅𝑞Fq.

    It was pointed out earlier that roots of irreducible polynomials over finite fields are not necessarily primitive elements of the corresponding extension fields as finite fields. Primitive elements of a finite field 𝐅𝑞Fq over its prime field 𝐅𝑝Fp are also called primitive polynomials6 over 𝐅𝑝Fp. Using such polynomials to implement extensions ensures that ――𝑥x― must be a primitive element in the extension field. Primitive polynomials of degree 𝑛n over 𝐅𝑝Fp can be obtained by factoring the cyclotomic polynomial Φ𝑛(𝑥)Φn(x) over 𝐅𝑝Fp.

    Theorem

    Let 𝑝p be a prime, 𝑛n a positive integer, and 𝑝 ⟂𝑛p⟂n. Also let 𝑑d be the order of element 𝑝p in the multiplicative group (𝐙/𝑛𝐙)×(Z/nZ)×. Then the cyclotomic polynomial Φ𝑛(𝑥)Φn(x) factors over 𝐅𝑝Fp into 𝜑(𝑛)𝑑φ(n)d primitive polynomials of degree 𝑑d over 𝐅𝑝Fp. In particular, Φ𝑛(𝑥)Φn(x) is irreducible over 𝐅𝑝Fp if and only if 𝑝p is a primitive root modulo 𝑛n.

    Proof

    Note that the roots of the 𝑛n-th cyclotomic polynomial are all 𝑛n-th primitive roots of unity over 𝐅𝑝Fp, and the degree of the minimal polynomial of an 𝑛n-th primitive root of unity 𝑑d is the number of its conjugates (including itself), which is the length of its orbit under the automorphism group ⟨𝜎𝑝⟩⟨σp⟩. So 𝑑d is the length of the orbit of the cyclic subgroup of {𝜁𝑖 :𝑖 ⟂𝑛}{ζi:i⟂n} under the map 𝜁𝑖 ↦𝜁𝑖𝑝ζi↦ζip, which is also the order of element 𝑝p in the multiplicative group (𝐙/𝑛𝐙)×(Z/nZ)×. If one does not want to rely on Galois theory, this can also be proven by showing that 𝑑d is the smallest positive integer such that (𝑥𝑛 −1) ∣(𝑥𝑝𝑑−1 −1)(xn−1)∣(xpd−1−1). Other conclusions are obvious.

    Although irreducible polynomials are very important for the implementation of finite fields, there is no good deterministic method to find an 𝑛n-degree irreducible polynomial over 𝐅𝑞Fq. In general, random methods can be used to generate such irreducible polynomials. Because among all 𝑛n-degree monic polynomials, irreducible polynomials account for Θ(1/𝑛)Θ(1/n), we can first randomly generate an 𝑛n-degree monic polynomial and then determine whether it is irreducible. This can find an irreducible polynomial after generating an expected Θ(𝑛)Θ(n) monic polynomials. Of course, such generated irreducible polynomials are not necessarily primitive polynomials, and the coefficients are not necessarily simple. In practice, if the size of the finite field is given in advance, one can often find primitive polynomials with simple coefficients by looking up tables7 to facilitate subsequent calculations.

    Reference Implementation

    This section provides a simple implementation of finite fields, for reference only. The code implements a method to randomly generate irreducible polynomials.
